summary: Proposes a stronger way to authenticate updates to the RIPE database using digital signatures based on PGP. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: Instead of a simple password to change an address book, you sign your changes with a special signature only you can make.

questions: how does pgp authentication work for ripe database
what is pgpkey auth in a mntner object
subtitle: How the RIPE database can check that an update was really signed by the maintainer, using PGP.

tldr.problem: The existing ways to authenticate RIPE database updates are weak: a MAIL-FROM header is easy to forge and a CRYPT-PW password travels unencrypted in the update mail.
tldr.mechanism: Maintainers store their PGP public key in a new key-cert object, point their mntner object at it with an auth value of PGPKEY-id, and then sign the whole update message.
tldr.outcome: The database software accepts an update only if the message signature matches a key named by the maintainer. It covers authentication only, not wider authorization.

facts.label: New auth value
facts.value: PGPKEY- followed by the key id

today: RFC 2726 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself calls its approach a first phase, with signature storage and other signing methods left for later.

sections.title: Why Stronger Authentication Was Needed
sections.content:
RFC 2726 proposes a stronger way to authenticate additions, modifications and deletions of objects in the RIPE database, based on digital signatures. The RFC says the existing methods have serious problems. MAIL-FROM relies on a mail header that is very easy to forge, and CRYPT-PW exposes the password to interception because it is sent unencrypted in the update mail message.

The goal was a signature mechanism built on widely available technology. PGP was the first choice, since it is in wide use and available both in and outside the US, and other methods may follow. The proposal came out of the RIPE DBSEC Task Force. It aims only at improved authentication, and does not cover authorization beyond what relates to authentication.
sections.eli5: Writing your name on a note is easy to fake, and a password sent in plain view can be copied. A signature that only you can make is much harder to fake.

sections.title: The key-cert Object
sections.content:
Key certificates are stored in the RIPE database itself, so users can query it and check the identity of the key used to authenticate a maintainer. A local keyring of public keys is kept for efficiency, holding only copies of certificates present in the database. Objects are created only through the existing e-mail mechanism (auto-dbm@ripe.net); the software never fetches a certificate from a key server.

A new key-cert object holds the certificate. Its name has the form PGPKEY-hhhhhhhh, the hex form of the four-byte PGP key ID, and the software checks that the certificate really belongs to that ID before authorizing creation or modification. Several attributes are generated by the software, and any submitted values are ignored: method (the string PGP), owner (one per user id on the key) and fingerpr (the key fingerprint). Because they are generated from the certificate, a querier can see the owner and fingerprint without importing the key, and can trust them as far as the database itself.

The certif attribute carries the ASCII-armoured certificate line by line, in the order submitted. The mnt-by attribute is mandatory, so a mntner object must exist first, and that mntner may not have auth set to NONE. Creating a key-cert adds the key to the local keyring, deleting it removes the key, and modifying it replaces the key, but only when the update is authorized.
sections.eli5: The database keeps a card for each person with a picture of their signature stamp. It fills in the name and a check number itself, so you do not have to trust what people write there.

sections.title: Changes to the mntner Object
sections.content:
The only change to the maintainer (mntner) object is a new possible value for its auth attribute: PGPKEY-<id>, where the id is the hex form of the four-byte ID of the PGP public key. It means the key in the key-cert object PGPKEY-id is used to check the signature of any creation, modification or deletion message sent to auto-dbm@ripe.net that affects an object this mntner maintains.

As before, auth can occur more than once. Mixing different methods, such as a PGP key and NONE, makes little sense. If there are several PGPKEY-<id> values, a signature from either key is accepted.
sections.eli5: The owner's record now says: if you want to change my things, sign with this particular stamp. If more than one stamp is listed, any one of them will do.

sections.title: Signed Updates
sections.content:
The whole message has to be signed. The software checks that the message is PGP signed, checks the signature is valid, and associates it with the objects in the message. A message may contain only one PGP signature.

If an object carries a mnt-by whose mntner has PGPKEY-<id> values in auth, the software checks that the object has a signature of the right type and that the ID of the signing key matches one of those values. The change is performed only if this authentication succeeds.

Signing the message rather than each object simplifies parsing. Per-object signing would let one message mix objects from different maintainers and allow storing signatures in the database for checking at query time, but storing signatures is beyond the first phase. The RFC also recommends checking that the mailer does not alter the text, for example by line-wrapping or turning tabs into spaces, and using only ASCII characters.
sections.eli5: You sign the whole letter, not each line. The post office checks the one signature at the bottom before doing what the letter asks, so do not let anyone retype or reflow your letter on the way.

sections.title: Requirements for PGP Key Certificates
sections.content:
No limit is placed on which PGP version made the key. Keys from versions 2.x and 5.0 are supported, and 5.0 keys are recommended. A submitted certificate must contain a signature of the key itself. It may contain other signatures, but the RFC recommends as few as possible, because the database does not talk to public key servers.

Anyone worried about trust should fetch the certificate from a public key server or another route and check the signatures there, comparing the key fingerprint, key type and length to be sure both certificates belong to the same key.

It is highly unlikely, but a key-cert with the same ID as a maintainer's key might already exist. If the existing key has been used and registered at key servers for a while, the person should contact the RIPE NCC at ripe-dbm@ripe.net and may have to create and register a new key.
sections.eli5: Only a few people should vouch for a key in the database. If you want to be extra sure, compare the key's check number with a copy you got somewhere else.

sections.title: Steps to Start Using PGP Authentication
sections.content:
Section 5 lists the tasks in order. A maintainer must:

  • Have a mntner object with an auth other than NONE, created the traditional way.
  • Prepare a key-cert object from their own key certificate, referencing that mntner in mnt-by.
  • Send the key-cert to auto-dbm@ripe.net, passing the authentication the mntner already requires (mail from a predefined address, or the correct password).
  • Change the mntner so its auth is PGPKEY-<id>.
  • Check all objects the mntner maintains; this is the only way to gain from the stronger method.
  • From then on, sign every whole update message that refers to those objects.
sections.eli5: First register your signature stamp, then tell the database to demand it, then use it on every request from now on.

sections.title: Example Objects
sections.content: The RFC shows a mntner and its key-cert together. The mntner AS3244-MNT has auth: PGPKEY-23F5CE35. The matching key-cert is named PGPKEY-23F5CE35, has method: PGP, an owner, a fingerprint, the armoured certificate in certif lines (from a version 2.6.2i key), and mnt-by: AS3244-MNT.
sections.eli5: The example shows a filled-in owner card and the signature-stamp card that it points to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is brief. The document addresses authentication of additions, deletions and updates to routing policy information through strong cryptographic means, and says the authorization of those transactions is addressed in RFC 2725. The RFC also notes that PGP is commercial software.
sections.eli5: This paper only checks who you are. Deciding what you are allowed to do is handled by a different paper.

items.label: PGPKEY-hhhhhhhh
items.desc: Mandatory, single; primary look-up key. Hex of the four-byte key ID.

items.label: Signing method
items.desc: Generated, single. For PGP the string PGP.

items.label: Key owner
items.desc: Generated, one per user id on the key.

items.label: Fingerprint
items.desc: Generated, single; hex bytes separated by spaces.

items.label: Certificate lines
items.desc: Mandatory; ASCII-armoured key, kept in submitted order.

items.label: Maintainer
items.desc: Mandatory; its mntner must not have auth set to NONE.
